parts.label: Part 3
parts.title: Does Class Size Matter?
parts.article:
Does Class Size Matter?
 
(A) Of all the ideas for improving education, few are as simple or attractive as reducing the number of pupils per teacher. Unlike competing proposals for reform, class-size reductions rarely elicit huge outcries or involve structural change. The testing of educators, by contrast, generally arouses the anger of unions. Similarly, establishing special 'charter' schools involves privileging some schools over others, with the credits provided usually coming out of the budgets of struggling local schools. With its uncomplicated appeal, class-size reduction in the U.S. has lately gone from being a subject of primary academic interest to a policy juggernaut with over twenty states aiming at decreasing class sizes.
 
(B) Do small classes improve school achievement? To answer this, investigators have attempted to analyse existing data, such as records at the U.S. Department of Education. These reveal that there were steep drops in pupil-teacher ratios between 1969 and 1997, but no significant gains in academic performance. But do these findings mean that class size makes no difference? Not necessarily. For instance, schools strive for more than just high test scores; they also usually try to keep their drop-out rates low. And, indeed, the drop-out rate for older students fell considerably over that period. Because drop-outs generally come from the low end of the achievement distribution, a reduction in the drop-out rate could be expected to pull down average test scores. Another reason for discounting those data is the difficulty of ensuring a level playing field. In a perfect world, U.S. students would all come from well-off families, with two highly educated English-speaking parents who are involved in their children's schooling. Teachers would all be creative and have complete mastery of the subject matter. The reality is very different.
 
(C) Over the past 35 years, some studies of existing data have produced evidence that smaller classes benefit students, but most of these studies were poorly designed. The exception was the Tennessee study called Project STAR (Student Teacher Achievement Ratio). Frederick Mosteller of Harvard University has called it 'one of the greatest experiments in education in United States history'. Students entering kindergarten were randomly assigned to one of three kinds of classes: a small class of 13 to 17 students, a regular-size class of 22 to 26 or a regular- size class with both a teacher and a full-time teacher's aide. The students remained in whatever category they had been assigned to throughout the third grade, after which they joined a regular classroom in the fourth. To ensure that teaching quality did not differ, teachers were randomly assigned to small and regular- size classrooms. Few teachers received any special training for working with small classes, and there were no new curricular materials.
 
(D) At the end of STAR, researchers analysed the data. Jeremy Finn of New York University and Charles Achilles of Eastern Michigan University found evidence for 'an array of benefits of small classes'. They calculated that students in smaller classes were outperforming their counterparts in regular-sized classes by the first grade and that this advantage persisted even after students returned to larger classes. They also found that the effect was stronger for black and Hispanic minority groups – a significant finding for policy-makers. Eric Hanushek of Stanford, however, criticises some of STAR's key conclusions. He argues that STAR does not prove that gains persist long after students return to regular classes. It was debatable how much later improvement stemmed from other factors, such as a supportive home. Nor does he accept that the benefits accumulate, with participants widening the gap with their peers in larger classes year by year. Hanushek and others have also shown that during the study too many children moved from regular to small classes, probably because school personnel caved in to parent demands. And Hanushek also asserts that STAR failed to ensure good randomisation of teacher and student assignments. However, these points do not undermine STAR's basic findings.
 
(E) The largest public class size reduction programme so far, California's, stands more as a warning than as worthy of emulation. That state is trying to reduce classes in kindergarten through grade three despite a shortage of teachers that is most acute in low-income areas. This is exacerbating the disparity in resources available to rich and poor schools in California, because more affluent areas can attract the best teachers. Indeed, some of the extra teachers needed are being recruited from the poorer schools. Researchers found a statistically significant achievement advantage in reading, writing and mathematics for students in classes that had been reduced to 20. What is more, the effect did not vary for students of different backgrounds.
 
(F) Wisconsin's Student Achievement Guarantee in Education (SAGE) was a five-year pilot study to do some of the groundwork for a major project. Class sizes were reduced in only 14 schools, but it was noteworthy for targeting schools at which 30% of the students were below poverty level, compared with California's across-the-board approach. SAGE lowered the average pupil-teacher ratio in kindergarten through third grade to 12–15:1 from 21–25:1. Analysts have studied the results of first-grade students in these schools and similar first-grade students elsewhere and found the results accord with those from STAR. STAR and SAGE have made it hard to argue against reducing class sizes. But the California initiative shows that reductions made with too little forethought can yield minuscule gains. Administrators need solid information before they can make sensible policy decisions.

questions.question: detailed criticism of the methodology of a project

analyses.content: 关键词 “criticism of methodology” 对应原文的 “criticises... does not prove... failed to ensure good randomisation”。
(Paragraph D) “Eric Hanushek... criticises some of STAR's key conclusions... asserts that STAR failed to ensure good randomisation...”
题目要求找对某个项目方法论的详细批评。D段提到 Eric Hanushek 批评了STAR项目的一些关键结论，认为它未证明收益持续、未能确保良好的随机分配等，这正是“detailed criticism”，选 D。

questions.question: a comparison of the data from class-size reduction projects

analyses.content: 题目要求找班级规模缩减项目数据的比较。F段提到分析师研究了SAGE的一年级学生结果，并发现这些结果与STAR的结果“accord with（一致/相符）”，这就是两个项目数据的比较，选 F。
“Comparison of data” 对应 “results accord with those from STAR”。
(Paragraph F) “...analysts... found the results accord with those from STAR.”

questions.question: the level of public interest in the issues of class-size reduction

analyses.content: 题目要求找公众对班级规模缩减问题的关注程度。A段提到该议题在美国最近已从主要的“academic interest（学术兴趣）”转变为拥有超过20个州参与的“policy juggernaut（政策巨轮/大势）”，反映了公众和政策层面的高度关注，选 A。
“Level of public interest” 对应原文的 “policy juggernaut... aiming at decreasing class sizes”。
(Paragraph A) “...class-size reduction in the U.S. has lately gone from being a subject of primary academic interest to a policy juggernaut...”

questions.question: details of action taken to protect the validity of a project

analyses.content: (Paragraph C) “Students... were randomly assigned... To ensure that teaching quality did not differ, teachers were randomly assigned...”
题目要求找为了保护项目有效性而采取的行动细节。C段详细描述了STAR项目如何通过“randomly assigned（随机分配）”学生和老师、限制特殊培训和教材等措施来“ensure that teaching quality did not differ（确保教学质量没有差异）”，即保护有效性，选 C。
“Protect the validity” 对应 “ensure that teaching quality did not differ / randomly assigned���。

questions.question: reasons why class composition changed during a project

analyses.content: 题目要求找项目期间班级构成发生变化的原因。D段提到在研究期间，许多孩子从常规班转到了小班，“probably because school personnel caved in to parent demands（可能是因为学校人员屈服于家长的要求）”，这就是原因，选 D。
“Reasons why class composition changed” 对应 “children moved... because... caved in to parent demands”。
(Paragraph D) “...too many children moved from regular to small classes, probably because school personnel caved in to parent demands.”

groups.description:
Reading Passage 3 has six sections, A-F.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A-F, in boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

groups.contentHtml:
32 The student composition of each class was left to chance.
33 A long-term improvement in performance was claimed.
34 Similar results were obtained for all social groups.
35 The project was a preliminary to a more comprehensive study.
36 Several different class types were involved in the project.
37 A special group of schools was selected to take part.
38 Classroom assistants were used as part of the project.
39 The project was responsible for aggravating existing problems.
40 Certain groups of pupils within the sample were identified as having benefited.

questions.question: The student composition of each class was left to chance.

analyses.content: 题目说每个班的学生构成是听天由命（left to chance）的。C段提到STAR项目的学生被“randomly assigned（随机分配）”到三种班级，randomly即left to chance，选 A。
“Left to chance” 是 “randomly assigned” 的同义替换。
(Paragraph C) “Students... were randomly assigned to one of three kinds of classes...”

questions.question: A long-term improvement in performance was claimed.

analyses.content: 题目说声称有长期的表现提升。D段提到STAR的结果显示优势“persisted even after（即使在之后仍然持续）”学生回到大班，即长期提升，选 A。
“Long-term improvement” 对应 “persisted even after students returned to larger classes”。
(Paragraph D) “...this advantage persisted even after students returned to larger classes.”

questions.question: Similar results were obtained for all social groups.

analyses.content: “Similar results for all social groups” 对应 “effect did not vary for students of different backgrounds”。
(Paragraph E) “What is more, the effect did not vary for students of different backgrounds.”
题目说所有社会群体的结果相似。E段提到California项目对于不同背景的学生，“the effect did not vary（��果没有差异）”，选 B。

questions.question: The project was a preliminary to a more comprehensive study.

analyses.content: 题目说该项目是一个更全面研究的初步/预备。F段提到SAGE是一个“five-year pilot study（五年试点研究）”来为重大项目做“groundwork（基础工作）”，选 C。
“Preliminary” 对应 “pilot study / groundwork”。
(Paragraph F) “SAGE was a five-year pilot study to do some of the groundwork for a major project.”

questions.question: Several different class types were involved in the project.

analyses.content: 题目说项目中涉及几种不同的班级类型。C段明确列出STAR有“three kinds of classes（三种类型的班级）”：小班、常规班、带助教的常规班，选 A。
“Several different class types” 对应 “three kinds of classes”。
(Paragraph C) “...assigned to one of three kinds of classes: a small class... a regular-size class... or...”

questions.question: A special group of schools was selected to take part.

analyses.content: (Paragraph F) “...noteworthy for targeting schools at which 30% of the students were below poverty level...”
题目说选定了一组特殊的学校参与。F段提到SAGE值得注意的是它“targeting schools（针对学校）”其中30%学生在贫困线以下，即选定特定群体，选 C。
“Special group of schools” 对应 “targeting schools at which 30%... below poverty level”。

questions.question: Classroom assistants were used as part of the project.

analyses.content: 题目说课堂助手（assistants）被用作项目的一部分。C段提到STAR的三种班级之一是“regular-size class with both a teacher and a full-time teacher's aide（全职教师助手）”，选 A。
“Classroom assistants” 对应 “teacher's aide”。
(Paragraph C) “...or a regular-size class with both a teacher and a full-time teacher's aide.”

questions.question: The project was responsible for aggravating existing problems.

analyses.content: 题目说项目导致现有问题加剧。E段提到California项目加剧了贫富学校之间的资源差距（exacerbating the disparity），因为富裕地区吸走了老师，选 B。
“Aggravating existing problems” 对应 “exacerbating the disparity”。
(Paragraph E) “This is exacerbating the disparity in resources available to rich and poor schools...”

questions.question: Certain groups of pupils within the sample were identified as having benefited.

analyses.content: 题目说样本中的特定学生群体被确认为受益者。D段提到STAR发现对于“black and Hispanic minority groups（黑人和西班牙裔少数群体）”效果更强，即特定群体获益，选 A。
“Certain groups... identified as having benefited” 对应 “effect was stronger for black and Hispanic minority groups”。
(Paragraph D) “They also found that the effect was stronger for black and Hispanic minority groups...”
